title: Inheritance and polymorphism
description: Public inheritance, virtual functions and override, object slicing, abstract classes and multiple inheritance.

content.title: Inheritance and virtual functions
content.body:
class Cat : public Animal { }; makes Cat inherit from Animal. With public inheritance, a Cat is an Animal: a Cat can be used through an Animal& or an Animal*.

Polymorphism only works for virtual functions. If Animal declares virtual std::string speak() const, a call through a reference or a pointer runs the version of the object's real type. Without virtual, the type of the reference or pointer decides.

In the derived class, write override after the function (C++11): the compiler then checks that it really overrides a virtual function of the base class.

content.explanation: pet is an Animal&, but it refers to a Cat, and speak is virtual: the Cat version runs. That is polymorphism.
Without virtual, the call is decided at compile time from the type of pet, which is Animal&. Unlike in Java, member functions are not virtual by default in C++.
This is object slicing: copy is a real Animal object, built from the Animal part of cat; the Cat part is sliced off. Polymorphism needs a reference or a pointer, like Animal& pet = cat.

content.question: Why write override on Cat::speak?

choices.text: The compiler reports an error if it does not really override a virtual function
Without it, the function cannot be called
It is required by every C++ compiler

content.explanation: A small difference, such as forgetting const or misspelling the name, silently creates a new function instead of an override. override turns that bug into a compile error.

content.title: Abstract classes and multiple inheritance
content.body:
A pure virtual function has no body in the base class: virtual double area() const = 0;
A class with at least one pure virtual function is abstract: it cannot be instantiated, and derived classes must implement those functions. C++ has no interface keyword: an interface is simply an abstract class with only pure virtual functions.

Unlike C# or Java, a C++ class can inherit from several classes.

A base class used polymorphically needs a virtual destructor, so that deleting an object through a pointer to the base runs the destructor of the real type. final forbids further inheritance.

choices.text: It does not compile: Shape is abstract because of the pure virtual function
s is a shape whose area is 0
It compiles, but calling s.area() crashes
s becomes an object of the first derived class

content.explanation: = 0 makes area pure virtual, so Shape is abstract. You create derived classes such as Circle and use them through Shape& or Shape*.

content.question: How many base classes can a C++ class have?

choices.text: One class plus any number of interfaces, like C#

content.explanation: class FlyingCar : public Car, public Plane { }; is allowed. It is powerful but can create ambiguities, so it is mostly used to combine interface-like abstract classes.

choices.text: Deleting a Cat through an Animal* without a virtual destructor is undefined behaviour; Cat's destructor may never run
Nothing, the Cat is destroyed correctly
It does not compile: new Cat() cannot go into an Animal*

content.explanation: Adding virtual ~Animal() = default; to the base class fixes it: delete then calls ~Cat() first, then ~Animal(). Any class meant to be a polymorphic base should have one.

content.instructions: Match each concept with its meaning.

pairs.definition: Lets derived classes override a member function, chosen at run time
Asks the compiler to check that a function overrides a virtual one
Makes a virtual function pure, without a body
Has a pure virtual function and cannot be instantiated
A class inheriting from several base classes
Copying a derived object into a base object loses the derived part
Forbids inheriting from a class or overriding a function
